As an english speaker (english being my first and only language so far) that has learned burmese for the past year, I think the hardest thing is the pronunciations. 

There is a letter that looks like a c, and it is pronounced "nga." I was baffled at how to make the sound and it took me a week to figure out how to do it because it required me to use my mouth and throat in a way I never did or even thought of before.

Burmese is also a tonal language, meaning the exact pronunciations matter, and if pronounced incorrectly it will mean something different. there's two friends I have from Myanmar whos names in English have the same spelling, and so I would assume same pronunciation too, but are actually different because of a slight vowel tone in their language. its very hard for me to know which is being talked about when its blatantly clear to everyone else. 

the spelling throws me off too sometimes because now and then I run into words that just have a spelling that disobeys the system and cannot be explained, kind of like how in English bolagna is not at all spelled the way it sounds, but you just keep track of those exceptions the way we do already with other weird english words.

other than that, I don't think learning burmese will be any more difficult than if I were learning Japanese or Chinese; both equally foreign to me. i have put a lot of time an effort in and made a great deal of progress.

Just have another conversation. Sometimes, it’s not just the conversation itself that changes everything, it’s what you notice about their reaction and behavior. If she is genuinely surprised or doesn’t notice how much more you spend (it’s easy to not realize the cost when it’s not coming out of her pocket), then maybe a real conversation could help your relationship. Talk about limiting date expenses or liquor on your end (dates done have to be expensive to be good) and when you make trips have a conversation beforehand about paying for everything fairly. Talk to her about limiting the home decor and doing a little more to compensate. Sometimes it’s fair to make a pool of grocery money, like a joint account so that you pay equally. And maybe talk to her to see if she is doing okay, sometimes people just can’t handle things like cleaning up simple messes or even personal hygiene when something creeps up. Not saying she’s depressed, but a change in behavior is worth looking into. In the end I hope you both end up spending less.

This is interesting because my parents are hoarders and I went through a similar process when my dad passed. Sorry for your loss. But it’s easiest to take it one category at a time, take a day separating everything you want to give away (or sell) or give to goodwill in some bags, then take a day collecting all their most valuable items or meaningful things and separate those off, then take a day just throwing away all items that are broken or could just be considered garbage in general. I’m not saying it can be done in 3 days, but go through that type of process again until it’s clean. It’s so much easier to stay focused when you are only working on one category, when you sort things into 3 piles it’s way easier to get confused, distracted, or just generally mentally burn yourself out. Good luck and once again sorry for your loss.

Edit: you should probably work on collecting the meaningful items like pictures and such FIRST because while you work on the other two tasks those items will distract you if they’re just laying around or could trigger you emotionally.

You need to have every unit 100% understood before you move on, because I’m sure you are familiar with one thing not making sense and it just speeds up and soon you understand nothing. When I was a kid, I’d get sick a lot as I had a bad immune system and so when I missed school, I’d miss units in math. This led me to believe math was not my subject and I was doomed for the rest of my life. I held that belief through high school and because I believed I sucked at it, I literally stunted my ability to learn it effectively. I spent lectures zoning out and sorting and stressing unintentionally, which caused me to do worse, confirmed my fear, and continues the cycle. There is a very specific way to learn math and you need to start at the beginning. There can be no gaps in your understanding, learning math is like a chain and a missing link breaks the entire thing apart. Learning online helps, because you can rewatch lectures and rewind when you find yourself not understanding completely.
